title: Git Commits
description: Learn how to make and manage commits in Git

content.overview: Commits are the fundamental building blocks in Git. They represent a snapshot of your project at a specific point in time. In this module, you'll learn how to create, view, and manage commits in Git.

steps.title: What is a Commit?
steps.content: A commit in Git is a snapshot of your project at a specific point in time. It includes all the changes you've made to your files since the last commit. Each commit has a unique identifier (hash) and contains metadata such as the author, date, and a message describing the changes.

steps.title: The Staging Area
steps.content: Before you can commit changes in Git, you need to add them to the staging area (also called the index). This is an intermediate area where you can select which changes you want to include in your next commit.

commands.description: Check the status of your repository
commands.expectedOutput:
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	hello.txt

behindTheCommand.title: How Git Tracks Files
behindTheCommand.content:
Git classifies files into three states:

1. **Untracked**: Files that Git doesn't know about yet
2. **Tracked, Modified**: Files that Git knows about but have been changed since the last commit
3. **Tracked, Staged**: Files that are ready to be committed

The `git status` command shows you which files are in which state.

steps.title: Adding Files to the Staging Area
steps.content: Use the `git add` command to add files to the staging area. You can add specific files or all changes at once.

commands.description: Add hello.txt to the staging area
Check the status of your repository
commands.expectedOutput:
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
	new file:   hello.txt

fileChanges.description: Git updates the index file to include the new file

steps.title: Creating a Commit
steps.content: Once you've added files to the staging area, you can create a commit using the `git commit` command. Each commit requires a message that describes the changes you've made.

commands.description: Create a commit with the staged changes
commands.expectedOutput:
[main (root-commit) xxxxxxx] Add hello.txt file
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 hello.txt

commands.description: Check the status of your repository
commands.expectedOutput:
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean

behindTheCommand.title: Anatomy of a Commit
behindTheCommand.content:
When you create a commit, Git:

1. Takes a snapshot of all staged files
2. Stores that snapshot as a new commit object in the .git/objects directory
3. Updates the current branch to point to the new commit
4. Each commit contains:
   - A pointer to the previous commit (parent)
   - A snapshot of the files at that point
   - Author and committer information
   - The commit message

steps.title: Viewing Commit History
steps.content: You can view the history of commits in your repository using the `git log` command. This shows you all the commits, starting with the most recent.

commands.expectedOutput:
commit xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx (HEAD -> main)
Author: Your Name <your.email@example.com>
Date:   Wed Jan 1 12:00:00 2023 +0000

    Add hello.txt file

steps.content: Let's make some changes to our file and create another commit.

Changes not staged for commit:

  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
